files.lesson.md: --- order: 7 unit: chance node: [AC9M7P01 n3, AC9M7P02 n1] title: Predict and test summary: "The expected number of times an outcome happens is its probability × the number of trials: 60 rolls should give about 10 sixes. Run the experiment and record the counts: the results come close, but rarely exactly." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Roll a dice 60 times and count the sixes. How many should you expect, how far off is normal, and when should you suspect the dice?" connection: chance-of-rain # data/connections/maths.yml (documentation only) app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8185 url: http://127.0.0.1:8185/index.html readySelector: ".ctally" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: chance.yml#pic, caption: "60 rolls: about 10 sixes expected (60 × 1/6). The actual count is near 10, but not exactly 10." } explainClip: query: { code: "@chance.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Expected count, then the real count" say: "Predict the count, then run the experiment." clip: - caption: { text: "P(6) = 1/6, so in 60 rolls expect 60 × 1/6 = 10 sixes.", say: "A six has probability one sixth, so expect ten in sixty rolls." } - wait: 600 - caption: { text: "Run 60 rolls, 10 at a time, and watch the count of sixes.", say: "Now roll sixty times, ten at a time." } - click: Run 10 - click: Run 10 - click: Run 10 - click: Run 10 - click: Run 10 - click: Run 10 - wait: 600 - caption: { text: "Close to 10, but rarely exactly: chance varies.", say: "Close to ten, but rarely exactly. Chance varies." } - wait: 1400 --- A fair dice, sixty rolls, and a count of sixes. Say what you expect before you see it. ## Predict: how many sixes? ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to the number of sixes in 60 rolls brings out the expected count, and whether they expect it to happen exactly." check: type: predict q: "You roll a fair dice 60 times. About how many sixes do you expect?" options: - "About 10" - "Exactly 6" - "About 30" - "You can't say anything" actual: "About 10: 60 × 1/6 = 10. The real count will usually be near 10, but not always exactly 10." ``` What fraction of rolls should be a six? ## Run: roll 60 times ```step stage: run insight: "Running 60 rolls and comparing the count of sixes with 10 shows that the expected count is a good guide, not a promise." try: { playground: board, starter: "chance.yml#run", height: 620 } check: { type: board, text: "Roll 60 times (press Run 10 six times). How many sixes did you get? Was your prediction right?", when: "t >= 60" } ``` A probability lets you **predict** what should happen over many trials: $$\text{expected count} = \text{probability} \times \text{number of trials}$$ So in 60 rolls of a fair dice you expect about $60 \times \tfrac{1}{6} = 10$ sixes. Then you **test** it: run the experiment, record the counts in a table, and compare. The **relative frequency** (count ÷ trials) is the experiment's estimate of the probability. Compare with others: did anyone get exactly 10? What was the furthest from 10? ## Investigate: expected and observed ```step stage: investigate insight: "Expected count = probability × trials; the observed count varies around it, and the relative frequency is count ÷ trials. Noah's mistake treats a small difference in a short experiment as proof the dice is unfair." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "You flip a fair coin 50 times. How many heads do you expect?" answer: "25" feedback: - ["50", "Only half the flips should be heads."] - ["0.5", "That is the probability. Multiply by 50 flips."] explain: "50 × 1/2 = 25." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#noah" text: "Noah tests a dice. Click the line where his reasoning goes wrong." answer: 4 fault: logic misconception: expect-exact explain: "Line 4: in 60 rolls the count of sixes often lands a few away from 10; 7 is common for a fair dice. The expected count is what happens on average, not every time. To test a dice, roll it many more times." - check: type: answer q: "In an experiment, a coin landed heads 13 times in 20 flips. What is the relative frequency of heads? (A decimal.)" answer: "0.65" form: decimal feedback: - ["13", "That is the count. Divide by the number of flips."] - ["13/20", "Right value: write it as a decimal."] explain: "13 ÷ 20 = 0.65, more than the probability 0.5: chance varies in 20 flips." ``` ### Expected, then observed Here is how to predict and test. ```worked P(6) = \tfrac{1}{6} :: The probability from the sample space. 60 \times \tfrac{1}{6} = 10 :: Expected count: probability × trials. \text{observed: } 7 \text{ sixes} :: Run the experiment and record the count. \tfrac{7}{60} \approx 0.12 :: Relative frequency = count ÷ trials, the experiment's estimate. 0.12 \text{ against } 0.17 :: Close but not equal: a short experiment varies. ``` Now: how many heads in 50 flips? ### Find the mistake Read Noah's reasoning. Is 7 instead of 10 surprising for a fair dice? ### Relative frequency ## Modify: one change at a time ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: a coin on the board, an unequal spinner, more trials, comparing two results, then the edge case of an expected count that is not a whole number." try: { playground: board, starter: "chance.yml#coin", height: 620 } tasks: - starter: "chance.yml#coin" hint: "Expected: 100 × 1/2 = 50 heads." check: { type: board, text: "Flip the coin 100 times. Compare the number of heads with the expected 50.", when: "t >= 100", explain: "Usually between about 40 and 60: close to 50, rarely exactly." } - check: type: answer q: "A spinner is $\\tfrac{3}{8}$ red. How many reds do you expect in 80 spins?" answer: "30" feedback: - ["3", "Multiply the probability by 80."] - ["24", "80 ÷ 8 = 10, then × 3."] explain: "80 × 3/8 = 30." - starter: "chance.yml#spinner" hint: "Red is 3 of 8 equal parts. Run 80 spins and look at the expected count column." check: { type: board, text: "Spin this spinner (3 red, 5 blue sectors) at least 80 times. Compare the reds with the expected count.", when: "t >= 80", explain: "Expected 30 reds in 80 spins; most runs land within about 8 of 30." } - check: type: question q: "Two students flip a coin 10 times each. Ana gets 7 heads; Ben gets 5. Is Ana's coin unfair?" options: ["Not necessarily: 10 flips is too few to tell", "Yes: 7 is not 5", "Yes: Ben's is the fair one"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "In 10 flips, 7 heads happens quite often with a fair coin.", "Both results are normal for 10 flips."] explain: "With 10 flips, results vary a lot. To judge a coin, flip it many more times." - check: type: question q: "Edge case: you roll a dice 50 times. What is the expected number of sixes?" options: ["About 8.3 (50 × 1/6): you can expect a value you can never actually get", "Exactly 8", "You can't expect anything because 50 is not a multiple of 6"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "8.3 is the expected count; real counts are whole, near it.", "The expected count does not have to be whole."] explain: "50 × 1/6 = 8.33…: an average over many experiments, not a count from one." ``` ### Flip 100 Each task changes one thing. ### An unequal spinner ### Test the spinner ### Two results ### Not a whole number ## Practise: expected counts ```step stage: practise insight: "Expected counts and relative frequencies in new contexts, mixed; the expect-exactly slip planted again; the review keeps sample spaces fresh." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "A bag has 2 red and 8 blue counters. You take one and put it back, 40 times. How many reds do you expect?" answer: "8" feedback: - ["2", "That is the number of red counters. Use P(red) = 2/10."] - ["32", "That is blue: 40 × 8/10."] explain: "P(red) = 2/10 = 1/5, and 40 × 1/5 = 8." smaller: check: { type: number, q: "Just the chance: 2 of the 10 counters are red. What fraction of the draws should be red? Give a decimal.", answer: 0.2, tolerance: 0.001, feedback: [[2, "That's the number of red counters. Out of how many counters?"]], explain: "2 out of 10 is 0.2. Then 0.2 of the 40 draws." } - check: type: answer q: "A spinner landed on green 18 times in 60 spins. What is the relative frequency of green? (A decimal.)" answer: "0.3" form: decimal feedback: - ["18", "Divide by 60."] explain: "18 ÷ 60 = 0.3." - check: type: question q: "Which result would make you most suspicious of a coin?" options: ["900 heads in 1000 flips", "6 heads in 10 flips", "52 heads in 100 flips"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "6 of 10 is very common.", "52 of 100 is very close to 50."] explain: "Over 1000 flips you expect about 500; 900 is far too many for chance." - check: type: answer q: "Review: roll a fair dice. What is $P(\\text{a number less than } 3)$? Simplest form." answer: "1/3" form: simplest feedback: - ["2/6", "Right: simplify it."] - ["1/2", "Less than 3: only 1 and 2."] explain: "{1, 2}: 2/6 = 1/3." ``` ### Expected count ### Relative frequency ### Suspicious ### Review: probability ## Make: plan an experiment ```step stage: make insight: "Choosing the number of trials for a target expected count reverses the lesson: trials = expected count ÷ probability." check: type: answer q: "You want to expect 25 sixes from a fair dice. How many times should you roll it?" answer: "150" feedback: - ["25", "That is the count you want. Each roll gives a six only 1/6 of the time."] - ["31", "25 × 6 = 150."] explain: "Expected sixes = rolls × 1/6, so rolls = 25 × 6 = 150." ``` Then: how many spins of the 3-red, 5-blue spinner to expect 30 reds? ## Make: on paper ```step stage: make insight: "Using the forecast chance on a run of days gives a second expected-count problem, set out on paper, with the key step (probability times trials) picked as the reason." check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "Over a school term, 40 days have a forecast of a 30% chance of rain (made up). About how many of those 40 days should have rain? Work it out on paper." steps: - ["$P(\\text{rain}) = 30\\% = 0.3$", "write the chance as a decimal"] - ["$0.3 \\times 40 = 12$ days", "expected count = probability × number of trials"] - ["Some terms will have 10 and some 14: 12 is the average, not a promise", "short runs vary"] picks: - step: 2 options: ["Multiply the probability by the number of days", "Add 30 and 40", "Divide 40 by 0.3"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "30 is a percentage, not a number of days. Chance times trials gives the count.", "Dividing by 0.3 would give the days needed to expect 40 rainy ones."] answer: "12" answerLabel: "Days with rain" tolerance: 0.05 feedback: - ["30", "That is the chance as a percentage. Out of 40 days, 30% is a smaller number."] - ["0.3", "That is the probability. Multiply by the 40 days."] - ["133", "That divides by 0.3. Multiply instead."] criteria: - "I turned 30% into 0.3 before multiplying." - "I multiplied the probability by the 40 days." - "I said 12 is what to expect on average, not exactly what will happen." explain: "0.3 × 40 = 12 days. Some terms will have a few more or fewer: the expected count is a guide." ``` Do this one in your book or on paper, one step per line, before you type the number. **Also used in** - **Weather.** "30% chance of rain" means that on about 3 of every 10 days with this forecast, it rains. - **Games.** A designer picks a spinner's chances, then predicts how often a bonus will come up in a session. - **Class work.** Run a spinner 80 times and compare the counts with what you expected. ```teacher summary: Students predict expected counts (probability × trials), run experiments on a chance board, record counts and relative frequencies, and see that observed results vary around the expected count (AC9M7P01 node 3, AC9M7P02 node 1). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 10 min · Investigate 12 min · Modify 12 min · Practise and Make 11 min goals: - I can predict how often an outcome should happen in a number of trials. - I can run an experiment, record counts and work out relative frequencies. - I can explain why results differ from predictions in a short experiment. struggle: "Expecting the count to land exactly on the expected value, and then calling a fair dice unfair after a short run. Ask: did everyone in the class get exactly 10?" before: > Do the Run board first. Students need Sample spaces and probability. The one idea: expected count = probability × trials; observed counts vary around it. The common mistake is expecting the predicted count exactly, and calling a fair device unfair after a short experiment; it is planted in Noah's reasoning. If you have real dice or coins, run the 60-roll experiment physically first and pool the class's counts; the board then lets students run far more trials than a lesson allows. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands; ask students who chose 'exactly 6' what 6 is." - "Run: collect everyone's count of sixes on the board as a dot plot; ask how many got exactly 10." - "Investigate: link relative frequency to Fractions, decimals and percentages." - "Modify: before the two-students question, ask what range of heads in 10 flips is normal." - "Make: ask for the general rule: trials = expected count ÷ probability." - "Paper: the forecast question is worked on paper; the page marks the number and the reason, then shows a model. Books out, and look at the pages." stuck: - see: A student expects the predicted count exactly (Noah's mistake). ask: Look at the class's counts. Did everyone get 10? fix: Expected means 'about, on average', not every time. - see: A student gives the probability as the expected count. ask: Out of how many trials? fix: Multiply the probability by the number of trials. stretch: Each of 30 students rolls a dice 60 times. Predict roughly how many of them will get exactly 10 sixes. Then simulate it with the board (about 1 in 7). support: Use the board's Expected count column to check each prediction. leads: > Next: Many trials (AC9M7P02 node 2): what happens to the relative frequency over hundreds and thousands of trials. Where it leads: simulating compound events (Year 8) and statistical significance much later. exit: q: A spinner has P(blue) = 0.4. How many blues do you expect in 50 spins? You get 23. Is the spinner unfair? a: 20 expected. 23 is close to 20, so there is no reason to think it is unfair. explain: > A probability predicts what happens over many trials: **expected count = probability × number of trials**. In 60 rolls of a fair dice, expect about $60 \times \tfrac{1}{6} = 10$ sixes. Then test it: run the experiment and record the counts. The **relative frequency** is count ÷ trials. In a short experiment the results vary: 7 or 12 sixes in 60 rolls is normal, so do not judge a dice on a few rolls. ```

# Noah's reasoning for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: noah
I rolled a dice 60 times.
P(6) = 1/6, so I expect 60 × 1/6 = 10 sixes.
I got 7 sixes, not 10.
So the dice must be unfair.
# endregion
